title: Giving and Receiving Feedback
keyIdea: Helpful feedback is about the work, not the person, and it is specific: it names one thing that worked (a star) and one thing to try next (a step). Vague comments like 'it's good' give nothing to use, and hurtful ones attack the person. When you receive feedback, listen first, ask a question if you are not sure what was meant, thank the person, and then decide: use it, ask about it, or set it aside if it does not fit your task.

kid: Feedback is what someone says about your work so you can make it better. It can help you a lot, or not at all. It depends on how it is said. Helpful feedback is specific. It names a part of the work. 'Your first line made me want to read on' tells the writer what to keep. 'It's good' is kind, but the writer cannot use it, because it does not say which part.
Good feedback is about the work, not the person. 'You're bad at spelling' hurts and gives no way to improve. 'Check how you spelled because in line 2' points to one thing to fix.
A simple recipe is a star and a step. The star is one thing that worked. The step is one thing to try next. Say both, and keep the step small enough to do.

When you get feedback, it can feel like someone is judging you. Try this order: listen to the end, ask if you are not sure, say thanks, then decide. You do not have to use every idea. If a tip does not fit your task, you can thank the person and set it aside.
adult: This lesson teaches two linked skills from the PSHE relationships strand and from classroom critique routines: giving feedback that is kind, specific and helpful, and receiving it without getting defensive. A star and a step (one thing that worked, one thing to try next) gives children a structure they can reuse in peer review, group work and home projects.

The most common slip when children give feedback is vagueness: 'nice', 'good job', 'make it better'. These feel safe but carry no information. A second mistake is confusing honesty with bluntness, as if being hurtful is the same as being helpful. Feedback that names the person ('you always', 'you're so') rather than the work is felt as an attack, so it is rarely used.

When receiving feedback, the typical reactions are to defend, make an excuse, blame the reader, or decide the whole piece is bad. Each one blocks learning. Model a calm script: 'Thanks. Which part lost you?' Asking a clarifying question is a sign of strength, not weakness.

A common misconception is that you must accept every suggestion. Children are allowed to judge feedback against their task: a tip to turn a persuasive letter into a comic does not fit, so they can thank the person and set it aside. Be careful to praise good choices about which advice to use, not only obedience. At home, give a star and a step on something low-stakes, such as a drawing or a Lego build, and ask your child to do the same for you. Then show how you respond when you get a step you did not expect.

familyTip: Swap a star and a step at dinner about something each person made today: a drawing, a meal, a game level. Keep the step to one small thing. Then each person says how they will use it, or why they are setting it aside.

visual.caption: Which kind of feedback is it? Drag each comment to a box, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: Your graph needs a title so I know what it shows.
The word 'creaked' let me hear the door.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: sort comments, build a star and a step, choose how to respond, and decide which tips fit your task.

practice.prompt: Which comment is the most helpful feedback on a poem?
choices: Your rhyme of 'light' and 'night' sounds great. Try adding a colour word in line 3.
practice.hint: Look for the one that names a part of the poem and gives a next step.
practice.explain: It gives a star (the light and night rhyme) and a step (a colour word in line 3). The others do not say which part.

practice.prompt: Your group gives {a} comments on your poster. {b} of them are vague, like 'nice'. How many comments are left that might be specific enough to use?
practice.hint: Vague comments cannot be used. Take them away from the total.
practice.explain: {a} take away {b} leaves {=a-b} comments that might name a part of the work you can use.

practice.prompt: Mia says, 'Your ending confused me.' What is the best first reply?
choices: It's not confusing, you just didn't read it properly.
practice.hint: Pick the reply that helps you find out what to fix.
practice.explain: Thanking and asking a question finds the exact part to fix. Blaming, giving up or hitting back all stop you learning.

practice.prompt: In peer review, each person gives a star and a step on {n} classmates' stories. How many stars and steps does each person give in total?
practice.hint: Every story gets one star and one step: two comments each.
practice.explain: {n} stories times 2 comments (one star, one step) is {=2*n} comments.

pool.prompt: Which comment is about the work, not the person?
choices: Your diagram labels are easy to read.
pool.hint: Look for the one that names part of what was made.
pool.explain: It names the diagram labels, a part of the work. The others judge the person.

pool.prompt: Why is 'Make it better' not helpful feedback?
choices: It does not say what to change or which part.
pool.hint: Could you act on it right now?
pool.explain: It is vague. Without a part and a next step, the person cannot use it.

pool.prompt: Your task is a letter asking the head teacher for a school garden. A friend says, 'Turn it into a comic.' What can you do?
choices: You must do it, or you are being rude.
Thank them and set it aside, because a comic does not fit the task.
Tell them their idea is stupid.
pool.hint: Check the tip against your task.
pool.explain: You decide which feedback to use. It does not fit a letter, so a polite thanks and setting it aside is fine.

pool.prompt: Which is a good star for a story opening?
choices: The short sentence 'Ava ran.' makes it feel fast.
pool.hint: A star names one exact thing that worked.
pool.explain: It names the short sentence and what it does for the reader. 'Add more words' is a step, not a star.

pool.prompt: You get feedback and feel cross. What should you do first?
choices: Explain why they are wrong straight away.
Listen to the end, then take a breath.
pool.hint: You can only decide about feedback you have heard.
pool.explain: Listen first. Feeling cross is normal, but defending or hitting back stops you hearing a tip that might help.

pool.prompt: Which is the best step to give on a poster about saving water?
choices: The writing is messy, as usual.
Add one fact with a number, like how much water a shower uses.
pool.hint: A step says one small, clear thing to try next.
pool.explain: It is specific and doable. 'More stuff' is vague, 'as usual' is about the person, and 'cool' is not a step.

pool.prompt: You get {a} tips. You use {b} of them and ask about 1. You set the rest aside. How many do you set aside?
pool.hint: Take away the ones you used and the one you asked about.
pool.explain: {a} take away {b} used and 1 asked about leaves {=a-b-1} set aside. Setting a tip aside is allowed if it does not fit.

pool.prompt: A class of {n} pupils works in pairs. Each pupil gives their partner one star and one step. How many comments are given in total?
pool.explain: {n} pupils times 2 comments each (a star and a step) is {=2*n} comments.

pool.prompt: Someone says, 'Your talk was too fast.' Which reply helps you most?
choices: Thanks. Was it the whole talk, or one part?
I was nervous, so it doesn't count.
pool.hint: Pick the reply that helps you find what to change.
pool.explain: Thanking and asking which part tells you exactly what to slow down. Denying, excusing or giving up all stop you improving.
